title: Iran stands firm on Hormuz plan after US rejection
gist: Iran's foreign minister says reopening the Strait of Hormuz remains contingent on its conditions (end of regional hostilities incl. Lebanon/Yemen, frozen-asset release, oil-sanction relief, end of the US naval blockade) after Trump rejected Tehran's seven-day plan relayed via Qatar. Iran enforces a ship-authorisation regime in Hormuz and fires on non-compliant vessels while the US sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas.

insights.claim: Iran has offered a 'seven-day plan' via Qatar under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened and normal maritime passage restored within seven days if its conditions are met.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete timeline for a potential oil-supply normalisation if a deal is struck; a binary catalyst for energy prices and shipping.
insights.quote: If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days.

insights.claim: Iran's conditions for reopening Hormuz include cessation of all Middle East hostilities including Lebanon (and Yemen), release of frozen Iranian assets, lifting sanctions on Iranian oil and an end to the US naval blockade.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Terms require large US concessions on oil sanctions, implying Iranian barrels returning to market in any settlement.
insights.locator: Iran's plan called for a cessation

insights.claim: Iran's Revolutionary Guards say they will keep 'punishing' the US until Iran's seven conditions are met, signalling the IRGC as a hardline veto player on any deal.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: IRGC rhetoric suggests continued attacks on shipping regardless of diplomatic signalling, sustaining risk premia.
insights.quote: We will not cease punishing the US until Iran's seven conditions are met.

insights.claim: Trump rejected the Iranian truce proposal, framing Iran's push for an immediate strait reopening as a sign that Iran is 'losing so badly'.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: US reads time as on its side, lowering odds of a near-term reopening.
insights.quote: They want to make a deal where they open the Strait immediately because they're losing so badly

insights.claim: Iran says mediators have not yet formally conveyed a US rejection, leaving a diplomatic channel technically open despite Trump's public statements.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Gap between public rhetoric and the formal mediator channel means deal headlines can still swing markets.
insights.quote: so far, nothing has been conveyed to us by the mediators

insights.claim: A June US-Iran memorandum of understanding to end the war and reopen the strait collapsed when Iran fired on commercial ships it accused of deviating from its approved route.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Shows how fragile agreements are: a single route dispute can unwind a deal, so any new truce deserves a heavy discount.
insights.locator: Washington and Tehran signed a memorandum

insights.claim: Iran requires ships to obtain authorisation before transiting Hormuz; non-compliant ships are regularly targeted and the US sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: A de facto Iranian permit regime keeps shipping insurance and tanker rates elevated.
insights.quote: Ships that refuse to comply are regularly targeted, while the United States sporadically bombs Iranian coastal areas in retaliation.

insights.claim: Iranian President Pezeshkian says Iran has not left the negotiating table but no longer trusts the United States given past experiences.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Trust deficit implies any deal needs front-loaded US concessions or third-party guarantees, prolonging disruption.
insights.quote: given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States

insights.claim: Saudi Arabia's foreign minister complained the international community has been absent in keeping both the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab open and rejected any party using the passages as a pressure tool.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Two chokepoints at risk simultaneously compounds Gulf export disruption, including Saudi rerouting options.

insights.claim: Russia's Sergei Lavrov offered that Russia stands ready to contribute to stabilising the region, positioning Moscow as a potential broker.
insights.speaker: Al-Monitor
insights.so_what: Russia, a beneficiary of high oil prices, seeking a mediator role is worth tracking for its incentives.
